utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, your Honours. Your Honours were asking about timing for the rebuttal evidence that the Prosecution would like to call and closing addresses. Our position on this is that, notwithstanding the fact that the Defence case may go into next week, we would still like to commence our rebuttal case on 5th November, that is, the Tuesday. We would like to commence our closing address around the middle of the next week which should be 14th November.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you know or can you give an estimate of how long you will need for rebuttal?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, the four days from 5th through to the Friday.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Including cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Have you estimated for cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you know how long you might require for your closing arguments?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: One day, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Wladimiroff? Is there anything else, Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. Rebuttal starting on 5th, that is not a problem for us, your Honour. We expect that we will need one, perhaps, two days of next week. Closing argument, though, starting on 14th November may cause some trouble for the Defence. You indicated 25th or 26th; we have a preference for 25th.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think I had indicated 21st or I have spoken about 21st which would be Thursday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, or 22nd would be fine too.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The 19th and 20th, the other Chamber will have the courtroom, that is, Tuesday and Wednesday. Could we begin on that Thursday then, 21st?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, 21st, Thursday. Indeed, that was no problem for us. The 25th and 26th would not be a problem either. We have a preference for 25th. May I add something, your Honour? The 14th is a problem for the Defence because not all members of the team will be available on that specific day. It is that specific day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps I might indicate, your Honours, that from the point of view of the Prosecution, whilst we would like to commence on 14th, we certainly would not want to be in a position where we do something on 14th and then there is a week delay or a break between that and any other part of the case. We would like the closing addresses to follow one after the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That will be fine with us, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What Miss Featherstone and Mr. Bos were saying to me is that the other Chamber may need more than two days. They may need three days. That would then get us into Thursday. Of course, if you are estimating a day and you are estimating, perhaps, one day also, that is awfully tight too. We certainly do not want to delay the completion over a weekend, unless you, gentlemen and ladies, want to return on the Saturday and we want to return on the Saturday. I do not know. Let me discuss it with the Judges. We can tell you later on. Why do you not call your next witness and then we will tell you how we might proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I call Dr. Wagenaar. DR. WAGENAAR, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please take the oath that is being handed to you in English, I think? We will find one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Professor, is your full name William Albert Wagenaar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Do you live in the Netherlands?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Do you hold the degree of PhD in Social Science from the University of Leiden where you prepared your doctoral thesis on Sequential Response Bias, a study on choice and chance in 1972?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Were you granted a Fullbright scholarship for the Pennsylvania State University during 1972 to 1974?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you been Head of the Psychology Department of the Institute for Perception of the Dutch National Foundation for Applied Sciences from 1974 to 1985, and in the same time part-time Professor of Applied Experimental Psychology at the University of Leiden from 1982 to 1985?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Were you appointed full-time Professor of Experimental Psychology in the section of Experimental and Theoretical Psychology of the Faculty of Social and Behavioural Sciences of the University of Leiden in 1985?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Is this still your present position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Have you been Dean of the Department of Psychology of that University from 1985 to 1987?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is called Head of the Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Have you been Head of the Department of Social Sciences of that University from 1987 to 1989?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and that is called Dean of the Department.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is called Dean.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot help it!

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Are you Head of the Section of Experimental and Theoretical Psychology of the Faculty of Social and Behavioural Sciences since 1985 until this present day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Are you Rector Magnificus or Vice Chancellor elect of the University of Leiden?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Has your work been concentrated on human perception and the functioning of the memory during the past 20 years?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, part of my work, not all of it, but much of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Are you a member of several Dutch, European and American academic and professional associations and societies and have you held offices in these organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Have you been a member or chairman of scientific committees and government advisory boards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Have you been an expert witness in trials involving questions of human perception and memory such as, for example, the Demjanjuk case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Have you extensively published in your field of expertise in scientific journals and books?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You call it "extensive", I can give you the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: More than 150 numbers, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Dr. Wagenaar, being a reputed expert on the functioning of human perception and the functioning of the memory, have you been asked by the Office of the Prosecution of the International Tribunal in March 1995 to advise the Prosecution about the memory of witnesses and the problems of identification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do not remember the exact date, but I think that is probably correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Without going into the substance of your advice to the Prosecution, did you suggest to the Prosecution that you would prefer to be appointed by the Court to act as an independent expert?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Were you informed by the Prosecution that such construction would not fit into the adversarial system?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did I contact you in October 1995 seeking your assistance for the same matter, that is, your professional opinion on the memory of witnesses and the problem of identification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did it become clear to you that I was not aware of your previous involvement with the Prosecution, and did you explain to me that you would prefer to be an independent expert witness making your expertise available to both parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you inform the Prosecution of your contacts with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, leading a witness through his background and credentials is one thing; testifying instead of the witness is another. I think my learned friend is leading at this stage.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It is simply a matter of ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is not really preliminary because I think that you, perhaps, want us to draw something from those conversations, so I will sustain the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What I will do, your Honour, is simply clarify the position of this expert witness to avoid any discussion on the matter and also to avoid the substance of any advice given to either party just to make it clear and that is all.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That really was my concern, just how far you are getting into that, because it is a leading question, but there is a greater concern that I had. OK. I will sustain the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I just want to see where I was left. [To the witness]: After having contact with me, Professor Wagenaar, have you informed the Prosecution about your contact with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you at any stage provide the Prosecution with an expert opinion on a photospread by a letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I wrote them a letter on 27th March 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Have you sent with the consent of the Prosecution a copy of that letter to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to show this letter for identification to the expert witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes, that will be marked as Defence what number?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: D90, as far as I can see it. (Handed). (To the witness): Is this the letter you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this letter as D90.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe we are talking about the same letter, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, would you show what has been marked for identification purposes as Defence 90 to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, there is no objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Defence 90 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Professor Wagenaar, did you also provide the Defence with an expert opinion on related matters by a letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I sent you a letter dated 10 October 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you spontaneously provide the Prosecution with a copy of that letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is mentioned at the end of my letter, I think, that I would send the Prosecution a copy of it or at the beginning of the letter, rather.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to show a letter for identification to the expert witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That will be Defence 91. Why do you not show it to the Prosecution? MR. WLADIMIROFF (To the witness): Is this the letter you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is the same letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I tender this letter as D91.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Defence 91 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Professor, do you refer in this letter D91 to the Defence to a document indicating the pages of the transcript in the Tadic case that have been given to you by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to show this document to the expert witness for identification, please. That will be D92. [To the witness]: Is this the document you refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, I tender this document as D92.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: What is that exactly? Is that a reference to transcripts that have been provided? Dr. Wagenaar, is that a letter from you to him or is that acknowledgment that he has received a letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It is a document provided by the Defence to the expert witness listing all pages of the transcript that have been given to the expert witness and also containing a summary of those statements.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Do you have a copy of that? Usher, would you show it to the Prosecutor, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: One moment, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Defence 92?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, your Honour. I should note, however, that in addition to listing pages and containing a summary of statements it also contains commentary provided to the doctor.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Defence 92 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Professor, did you get a full transcript of all pages indicated in the document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Is your opinion as given in the letters, Exhibit D90, your letter to the Prosecution and D91, your letter to the Defence, as well as the evidence you are about to give today based upon the materials given to you by the Prosecution and the Defence, and your personal knowledge drawn from your own work and that of other recognised scholars in your field of expertise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: From the pages of the transcript as listed in document Exhibit D92 that I have given to you, it appears that in court two specific terms were used during the trial, "identification" and "recognition". Can you tell the Court what these terms mean in psychological and forensic literature?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Recognition" is a very broad term that is used for any situation in which stimulus is shown to a person, in which a person has to express whether he or she has seen that stimulus before. So that could be a face, a person, a book or words, a picture, anything. In principle, all identification procedures that are used in court proceedings or in police investigation would fall under that broad definition. I have noticed in the pages from the records that I have seen that this Court has adopted a slightly different meaning of the word in which it has distinguished between "identification", which is a word that is normally not used in psychological theory, and "recognition", where recognition has been reserved for those witnesses who know the accused before the war and who have later identified him; whereas "identification" has been used by this Court to indicate subjects, witnesses rather, who did not know the accused before the war, and who have identified him by the means of a photospread. In order not to confuse matters, I have suggested in my letter that I follow this terminology, that I will use "recognition" for the recognition of a person that was known before the war to the witnesses and "identification" by those recognitions by witnesses who did not know the accused before the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. If the term "identification" was used in Court in connection with witnesses who did not know Mr. Tadic before the war and who identified him with the use of a photospread, would such identification always prove that the accused committed the crime with which he is charged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, definitely not. Maybe it is, if I may, it would be good to explain the logic of an identification test ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If you would, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- and what it purports to do. A proper identification test usually has the objective to place the accused at the scene of the crime. I mean the following. If the witness has never seen the accused before the moment of the crime and possibly at the scene of the crime, depending on whether the accused was there or not, then a later identification that would follow all the rules for identification would logically place the accused at the scene of the crime, because how can a person recognise, identify, someone if he or she has never seen that person? If there is only one occasion in which he or she can have seen that person, then, logically, it is confirmed that that person was present at that particular occasion, in this case the scene of the crime. It does only that; it locates the accused at the scene of the crime. It does not say what the accused did there, whether he was guilty of any crime or not. It only positions him at the scene of the crime. So it can definitely never confirm what that person did. That is a different question. It only contributes one step, locates the person at the scene of the crime. It can only do that if the identification procedures were correct. There are many ways in which identification procedures can be incorrect and usually when you make an error in the procedure, the logic -- you lose the logic that the result places the accused at the scene of the crime. For instance, if there has been another encounter between the witness and the accused, you cannot logically conclude that since the accused was recognised, there is only one explanation which is an encounter at the scene of the crime. There is another explanation which is the second encounter. So, as soon as you know that there was a second encounter, you lose the logic of the identification test. In my letter to you and also in my published work, I have discussed many problems in identification procedures that I would say almost without exception reduce or either remove the logic of the test. So my answer is, no, an identification test will never prove what the person did. It can only prove that the accused was at the scene of the crime, but that will only happen if there were no flaws in the procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Does it mean, what you have just told us, that an identification by an eyewitness does not always have probative value?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it very much depends upon the specific conditions in which the test was made. To give you one example, if the witness knew the accused even before the crime, the identification does not logically lead to the conclusion that because of the identification we can now know that the accused was at the scene of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Am I right ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the test was highly suggestive in one way or the other, again there is another explanation for the correct identification of the accused, namely, that it was highly suggestive -- it is too easy, anybody, even those people who were not present at the scene of the crime, would find it easy to find out to whom they should point in the test.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking then that the probative value of an identification might generally be crippled by two major issues: First of all, is there any reason to believe or to take into account that the witness knew the accused from other occasions than the crime and, secondly, was the procedure of identification correct? Are these the two major issues there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would say the logic that the identification proves the presence of the accused at the scene of a crime is crippled by those things. You may have other objectives with an identification test. For instance, simply to verify that we are still talking about the same person, the same person that these people knew so well from many years before the war, just to exclude the mistakes or so, and that still could be very useful. But that is a different thing than the logic that possibly the test places the accused at the scene of the crime. It is that logic that is crippled by the two things that you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. If the term "recognition" was used for witnesses who knew Mr. Tadic before the war and who recognised him in Court as the person they had known for a long time, would such recognition always prove that the accused committed the crime with which he is charged?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I would say if they knew him very well before the war, a recognition during the investigation only proves that they knew him very well before the war. If there is any reason to doubt that, we have now established that. But anybody who knew him very well before the war would be able to recognise him after the war. So, logically, that does not prove that their testimony about what happened during the war is true or not true. It simply has nothing to do with it logically.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Does this mean that recognition of an accused does not always have probative value then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it proves what it proves. It proves that they know this person, and that is what they said. If that needs proof, it has probative value. If you want to prove through the recognition that their testimony about what happened during the war is true, I would say it cannot contribute anything to that, apart from the fact that, apparently, this witness has not lied about his previous acquaintance with this person. If it is worthwhile to establish that, it does it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Are there major problems here that might cripple the probative value as such, that is, simply, "We know him for a long time and, therefore, we are able to recognise him"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not quite understand your question. I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Are there problems here you could label that might cripple a claim of a witness ,"I know him from before and, therefore, I am able to recognise him"? Are there procedures that might cripple or is there anything that might cripple?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in principle, these what you call "recognitions", identifications by people who knew him from before the war, in principle, the identifications were done here in the courtroom. They are what we call "dock identifications". Of course, the situation here is very simple. It is very easy to find out who of the persons present in this courtroom is the suspect, is the accused. So even if they lied about knowing him before the war, they would find it easy to identify him now. So if you have really a doubt whether it is true that they knew him before the war, I would say a better test is needed than a dock identification test. On the other hand, assuming that these witnesses are totally honest, and there would have been a mistake, so the person they described is not the person present in the courtroom today, there is every reason to assume that they would now correct the mistake and say, "No, that is not the person I mean". They have given all opportunity. Only when you start to doubt their sincerity or their honesty, you need a more critical test than a dock identification. But I have in the discussions I have read not seen any description about whether it is true that they lived in the same village or in the same area. So I would not directly see a need for a more strict test than just a kind of verification test in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I take it then that "identification" and "recognition" in the way it has been used in this Court require two different forms of testing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. For those few witnesses who did not know him before the war, you need a much more strict and better controlled test, because the outcome may have the logical implication that now the accused is placed within the camp. I would say that conclusion is so important there must be no doubt about that the evidence is doing that. So that is why for those who did not know him and who are going to pass an identification test, a very well controlled procedure is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Could you describe such a procedure for us, just in general terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say I have described it in length in various publications. The surprising thing is that although you might think it is easy to do, in fact, it is not at all easy to do. I have published in 1988 50 rules for such tests. That is not a limited list. There are more rules. Those are the 50 most important ones. In principle, what you do is that you place the person whom you suspect among a number of other people whom are known to be innocent and are known to be unfamiliar to the witnesses, who sort of fit the same general description as the suspected person. Then you ask the witnesses whether they recognise the one person they have described before or not. You tell them that maybe that person is not in the lineup so they should not guess. They should only point at someone if they recognise him positively. You tell them they can only point at one person because they cannot recognise two, at one person or at nobody. You give them a limited time to do that because if you recognise them, you recognise them in a short time, it does not help to wait two and a half hours and then you may recognise them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What kind of testing is generally required for what has been called in this Court "recognition"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, if -- it depends on, as I said, it depends on what the purpose, the objective of what the recognition is. If it is just to verify that this is the same person that the witness described, the person has known for so long, then in Court dock identification probably would suffice. If there is sincere doubt that this person, although he claims to have known the accused for a long time, in fact never had met him, then also for that purpose you need a far more critical test like the one I described to you. But if it is not at issue, if it is not in doubt whether he knew that person, you do not need to take all those precautions. You only need to verify that we are still talking about this same person so there are no mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Professor, before I ask you about the tests that were applied in the Tadic case, let me first ask you, did you find in your review of the transcript that 52 witnesses were confronted with the accused in one way or another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on page 3 of my letter of 10th October, if I may refer to that letter because it is more practical, I think. There is a table which lists the number of witnesses ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Before you do that, Professor, may I suggest that we provide the Court with a copy of that letter that might be helpful for you to follow the explanation? (Handed) Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So on page 3 there is a little table that represents the witnesses about whom I have read parts of the records. I do not want to imply that these are all the witnesses that have been presented to the Court. Those are the witnesses that I know of on the basis of this package, this extract, of the Court proceedings. Of these 52, 48 declared that they knew Mr. Tadic long before the war and four declared that they did not know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Out of those 48, can you explain to the Court how many of those 48 did recognise Mr. Tadic or did recognise him and their conditions that would be correct if the test was applied to the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends what the objective is. Out of these 48, 42 identified -- no, 47 identified the accused here in the courtroom. If the objective of that is just to make sure there is no misunderstanding, it confirmed they recognised him, it confirmed, "This is the person I am talking about", that would be a correct procedure for just verifying that there is no gross mistake. Five additionally also looked at photographs before they came to Court, but generally (and I have described that in this paragraph relating to this), these photo identifications were not proper photo line ups. Some of them consist of only two photos. So again also these five, about these five, we know that they verify that the person being accused now is the person they were talking about, and about which they declared that they knew him long before. Nothing else. Then there is one witness who appeared in Court, but I could not find any identification attempt. So we do not -- the verification was not done. I would say, in principle, with this 47 there is nothing wrong as long as the logical conclusion of those identification that is drawn by either you, the Prosecution or the Court is not that those identifications now place the accused at the scene of the crime, in the camp, because they cannot logically do that. It is only established here in Court the witness still thinks that the person he is talking about is the same as the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So you did find 48 witnesses who claimed that they did know Dusko Tadic before the war, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and maybe I should add that a proper lineup, the way I described, is impossible with people who knew him anyway, because even if they had never seen him during the war they would find it easy to identify him. So the logic, the logic of the proper identification test, would be lost anyway. So, I think the procedures that have been used here are adequate for the limited purpose, the limited objective, of simply excluding gross mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May I try to sum this up? Did you find 84 witnesses who claimed that they knew Mr. Tadic before the war, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would say, rather, 48.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: 48, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right. Did you find that 42 of these 48 witnesses claimed that they recognised Mr. Tadic in the dock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, 47. You have to add the five, those five.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I will come to that letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK. 42 identified him, as far as I know, only here and not before with the help of photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you find that five of these 48 witnesses recognised Mr. Tadic by use of a photospread and also recognised him in the dock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I should say, of course, that since they have seen photographs of him before, there is a slight logical problem here, because if, in fact, they had never seen him before the war but only on this photograph, they would also find it possible to identify him here in Court, and certainly for those five it does not really prove that they knew him before the war because they have seen his picture during the investigations. But if you want to assume that those witnesses are honest people, they would have had -- and there is a mistake, just that the wrong person is here, then of course they would have said, "No, this is not the person I have known for so long".

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you find that one witness who had failed to recognise Mr. Tadic in the photo test was subsequently asked to identify him in the dock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Can you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you find that one witness who failed to recognise Mr. Tadic in the photo test was subsequently asked to identify him in the dock?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Wait a minute, you are not referring to the one in my table where it says one person, I think, because that is a person for whom there was simply no identification attempt whatsoever, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Perhaps you could read to the Court in your expert opinion the sentence beginning with "The one exception"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is on page 3 I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: On page 3, a little over the middle of the page. At the end of the sentence you will see "The one exception". It is at the top of that letter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "With the exception of one, the 40 tests revealed positive results".

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Later on down five lines down you will find at the end of line ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. "The one exception mentioned above was a witness who participated both in the photo test and the dock identification." OK, yes, that is the witness who failed in the photo test and later she claimed that in fact she had recognised Mr. Tadic but had failed to express that. That is a problem because if one wants to stick to the rules for identification the first response, that is the final response. You do not allow witnesses to correct their responses, and definitely not after a while when they have seen and talked to other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Should a subsequent dock identification then be held after such a test or failed test?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle not I would say. This is a person who, according to the rules, has demonstrated that she cannot easily identify the witness. In a subsequent dock identification, as I explained, it would be rather easy for her because she has seen the picture. Of the 13 pictures she has seen, if she has had the complete test, there is one person present, so it is easy for her to realise that is the person she should point at. So the answer is, no, once there is doubt whether a witness can identify the accused, once the witness has failed to do that, I would say you should reject the witness and note it as a non-recognition, non-identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would you say then that that dock identification of that witness fails diagnostic value?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The dock identification does not have the power to sort of correct what was lost during the first identification.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I just ask a question about that one person? Is that person in your number for the photo test or is that person in the number for the dock identification or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the person -- she is in the five.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: She is in that five?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She is one of those five because she received two tests.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: She is listed as a dock identification ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And photo test, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: --- but for someone who knew him. Is she also in the four? No, she could not have been because she knew him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, she knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: She is in the five.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: She knew him but she could not recognise him in the 13-picture photo test. So she is within those five.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: She is in the dock identification. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So where does that leave us? How many positive recognitions were there altogether of those who claimed that they knew him before the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So from those who knew him before the war, those 48, 46 recognised him in one way or the other. One as far as I know was not tested and one did not pass the test.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Again, Professor, before focusing on the ins and outs of these recognitions in details, does this mean that these 46 recognition logically corroborate the claim of these witnesses that Mr. Tadic is the person they have seen to commit the crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, logically it corroborates that that is the person they know as Mr. Tadic. They are able to indicate who Mr. Tadic is. I would say that is a necessary condition for believing that they saw, that they know who saw commit some crimes. So, if they would not have passed the test there would have been a problem with legal evidence, because if they cannot recognise him how do they know that that was the person they saw commit crimes? It is a necessary condition. They should pass the test, but once they have passed the test there is still a question about: Is it true what they say about him? They know who it is. Of course they know if they have lived in the same village. So they are not lying about knowing who he is. That is all that is proved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Are you saying it does not logically corroborate the claim of these witnesses that Mr. Tadic is the person they have seen to commit the crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, logically not, because others who have lived in the village and who have never seen anybody do any crimes would found it equally easy to identify him. So the easy identification by people who are from the same village or same area, just means they are from the same area, that is all. It does not mean that they saw or did not see any crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If we proceed to the other group, those who claim that they did not know him before, how many people did you find out of those 52 witnesses according to your review?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found four in the pages that were given to me. I consider these four, although the number might seem small, are extremely important because if the procedures are correct then, logically, that places the accused in the camp. I think that is such an important element to the Court that, even although there are four, I would say four is a small number compared to 52, but it is not a small number. There are four witnesses who all attested they have seen him in the camp, and if they can now recognise him and the tests were executed in the correct manner, there is no other explanation for the recognition but the fact that they saw him in the camp. So those four, it is not a small number. They are extremely important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, may I ask a question? You say these four are very important because of placing him in the camp. If you look back to the 42 some of them knew him from childhood, we will assume. They say, "We saw him in the camp". Why is that evidence less important than the evidence of the four, if the test for the four is properly conducted? I do not follow that at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I am not saying that evidence is less important. What I am saying is if they tell you, "We saw him in the camp", and you want to confirm that because you do not believe those statements, then the identifications do not help you any more. If you do not believe what they said about seeing him in the camp, then asking them to identify him does not help you. It does not add anything. If you want to believe what they said, you do not even need the identifications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But we are not using identification to determine whether these witnesses are truthful or not. That is quite a different matter, a matter for the Court, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure, but that is exactly the reason why of those 42 or 48 depending on to whom you want to refer, their identifications do not add anything to their truthfulness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: No, but it may not be intended to. It has nothing to do with truthfulness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I follow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Whereas the four, that is a different matter. On the basis of their identification you may decide whether they are truthful or not, because if they are not truthful it will be impossible for those four to identify him, you see. So there logically it has a different meaning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So, do these identifications of those four logically place Mr. Tadic at the scene of the alleged crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They have the potential to do that, depending on whether the procedures were applied correctly or not. But they have the potential to do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So without correct procedures they do not have that potential?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If there are really gross violations of procedures, that potential is lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking then that the value of these four identifications totally depends on the procedure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Professor, would it be relevant to know about other photo tests with persons who were interviewed by the Prosecution or other investigating bodies and who have not been called by the Prosecution to give evidence in court? Would it be relevant to know about the other photo tests?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, definitely for various reasons. One is that on the basis of these four witnesses I could not form a clear image of the procedures, the exact procedures that have been used, and maybe if there were more witnesses that, bit by bit, details of those procedures would come out. That is one. But the more important factor is that the one thing you definitely want to know is whether there were witnesses who participated in the photo test and who did not recognise him. Now the score, if I may say so, stands four out of four. Four represented the photo test, they all identified him. If one would believe that those witnesses were lying about, say, their experiences and were simply guessing in the test, then this result would be highly unlikely. It would be 1/13th to the power of 4 which is an incredibly small number. If in fact these four witnesses are four out of, say, 50 for example, and the other 46 did not recognise him but we are now told about them, then certainly the likelihood that four out of 50 would guess correct is rather high. So if we want to exclude the possibility that people were simply guessing and guessed correctly, then we have to know how many witnesses participated in such tests, in total and what the results of all of them were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What if one of these four or all of them would have seen a photo, a previous photo test with the photo of Dusko Tadic in a different setting, in another case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That would invalidate the test because then we cannot decide what it means that they recognised him. Does it mean that they saw him in the camp because that was the only encounter? Or does it mean they remembered from the previous photo? So the logic then, the logic of the test has gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Let me focus on the major problems that might cripple the outcome of your review. I take it that a photospread should not contain such suggestive details or biasing elements that you would say that such a test is not sufficient to identify a suspect, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all details that make it very easy to guess who the suspect in that lineup is, in principle invalidates the test. The rule is, which is a very practical rule, that if you ask people who were never involved in this whole problem to indicate who they think the accused is, they should not be able to do that. If they understand from some suggestive aspect of the lineup who the accused is, then certainly it does not mean anything any more that the witnesses can do the same. It does not prove they have seen him because others who have not seen him can do it equally easy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Is there a test in your field of expertise that enables you to test whether the photospread is correct or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is sometimes referred to as the Doob and Kirshenbaum test and I have, as well as we could, applied that test to the set of 13 pictures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What does the test mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I reported this to Mr. Tieger in my letter of March 27th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May I then suggest we present a copy of that letter to the Court. Can you tell us what this test means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The test consists of presenting the 13 pictures to we call them "subjects", or you might call them naive witnesses but I would rather call them subjects because they have nothing to do with the trial, and ask them: "One of these people is accused of being a war criminal. Have you any idea who it is?" We asked 39 subjects and their choice frequency can be found in the little table on page 3 of my letter. The picture of the accused is No. 3. So what you can see is that five out of 39 selected the accused. The guessing level is three out of 39, 1/13th. So it is slightly above the guessing level, but not significantly so. I reported in my letter that there is a problem with this test which could not be mended by me easily, which is that my subjects had the Dutch nationality, whereas the witnesses definitely had not. The problem is, and this is an hypothetical problem because at that time I could not find out how big the problem was, the problem is that imagine that people from the former Republic of Yugoslavia can easily distinguish between the various ethnic groups, and imagine additionally that Mr. Tadic is the only one who clearly looks like a Serb and the others do not. Then to people from my subjects that would be not be obvious. They would not select the picture of Mr. Tadic as the only one representing a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: By your subjects you mean Dutch?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My Dutch subjects. Witnesses who look at those things and who come from the former Republic of Yugoslavia might immediately recognise there is only one Serb in the lineup and say, "Ah, that must be him", because the person we are talking about is a Serb. I could not easily mend that because I had no people from the former Republic at my disposal as subjects. I reported this problem. Since then we have run experiments in Belgrade with subjects -- I still call them subjects because it has nothing to do with the trial as such -- with subjects who are more or less representative of, say, the group of witnesses. What we have found is that also these subjects found it impossible to classify the pictures according to ethnic background, which suggests to me that this problem, hypothetical problem, did in fact not occur. Again I must say there is an exception there too. I believe I must apologise to make things so complicated as scientists always do, but that is my profession. I cannot help it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Please do tell the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me take a very extreme example. Imagine that we would have presented 12 pictures of Japanese people to those subjects in Belgrade and asked them, "Group them according to ethnic background", and then mention the Yugoslav groups like Croats, Macedonians and so on. They would find it extremely difficult to group the Japanese faces in these categories because they simply do not fit. Of course, what you have to know is that the pictures that you present are of people from the former Republic of Yugoslavia. So that the question to categorise them, to classify them, is a meaningful question. Unfortunately, I do not know who these 12 people, these foils in the set of 13, who they are and where they came from. So if they are not Yugoslavians at all, one reason why they could not be classified according ethnic groups is that they simply do not belong to these ethnic groups. That is a question I have to leave open. I do not know who they are and there is no easy way for me to find out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Does it mean that your experiments in Belgrade depend on the assumption that those foils were people from the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: And, if not, that this test in Belgrade does not add anything to your test with Dutch subjects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have invited a scientist. It is more complicated, but the question is not are they from the former Yugoslavian Republic or not but how many. If one is not I would say there is still no problem. If only one is a former Yugoslavian then there is a problem. So it is matter of degree. But I would say it would be very nice to be assured that they all came from the former Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Actually did you show all 13 pictures to the subjects in Belgrade or a lesser amount of pictures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we asked them to classify the 12, not the picture of Mr. Tadic, because we assumed that by now they would recognise this picture immediately and know that he is from the former Serbia. So that would be a meaningless question. We also did not want to suggest to them that what they were doing would contribute to this trial, because that could give them all sorts of second thoughts, second reasons, to answer to our questions instead of simply doing the task, which is classifying according to ethnic background. So we did not show that picture. It would not teach us anything that would be useful, and it would sort of threaten the neutrality of the test.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: By now what do you mean, when would it be no longer appropriate to run the test when the trial started or at an earlier date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it would be very nice before the photospread was shown to anyone at all to test it thoroughly to see that it is not biased, to see that naive subjects from the group who was going to be interviewed later, people from Bosnia, that they would find it impossible, not having met Mr. Tadic before, to identify who the accused in that lineup is. That would be very nice. It would be a very wise precaution. Now it is of course impossible to do that with naive people from Bosnia because I assume that there are very few people in Bosnia who do not know about this trial and who have not seen in one way or another the face of Mr. Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking then that usually the Doob and Kirshenbaum test is performed with the same ethnic group as the accused? Is that the condition, a logical condition?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a logical condition, the same people drawn from the same populations as where the witnesses come from. That is the ideal condition, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Do I understand you well that you are not able to tell the Court whether the test was run with the same group as the accused when you tested the photospread of the Prosecution? You simply do not know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Wait a minute, maybe there is a confusion now. I thought you were asking about subjects in the Doob Kirshenbaum test as compared to witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am asking you ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. Now you are asking about the foils coming from the same ethnic background ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- as the accused, which is a totally different question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question then. Is it usually done to run a Doob and Kirshenbaum test with foils of the same ethnic group as the subjects you run the test with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not necessary. It is perfectly possible that the witnesses are, say, Japanese and the accused is a Serb. There are two conditions that you would ideally meet, which is your naive subjects in the Doob and Kirshenbaum test should come from the same population as the witnesses. Second, the foils should come from the same ethnic background as the accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But these two groups can be entirely different. The witnesses can be all Japanese and the accused and the foils can be all Croats or Serb or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Do you know who composed the photospread that was used in the Tadic case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have only hearsay information about that. I am not sure that you want to know that. The pictures were given to me by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was there any information added to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One could not obtain information about who these foils were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you ask whether there was any information about that available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was told that those 12 were provided by the Dutch police, but I have no way to verify that. I have talked to the person in the Dutch police organisation who was involved in that and who confirmed he had anything to do with it, but he could not give me any details about who these 12 were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Was there any registration of who those people were, names, ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If there is it was not given to me. I have asked for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It was not available?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot say that. It was not made available to me when I asked for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Am I right then that you do not know anything about the ethnic background of the foils?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would the presentation of a photospread containing photographs of, let us say, Bosnian Muslims or Croats or even non-Yugoslavs to non-Serb witnesses invalidate the choice of frequency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, can you ask that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would the presentation of a photospread containing photographs of Bosnian Muslims or Croats or non-Yugoslavs to non-Serb witnesses, say, Muslims or Croats, invalidate the choice of frequency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not necessarily. I would say it all depends on the test. That is exactly why you run such a test to make sure that the photo set is chosen correctly and whether people from the relevant population find it easy to identify who the accused is. If they do not the test is correct and then it really does not matter where they came from. But that test, the Doob and Kirshenbaum test, run with people from Bosnia, Bosnian Muslims, cannot be run any more because they know who Tadic is. The replacement, the best, the next best, the test I did, had the test of the 12 foils without the picture of Tadic, for that test it is important that we know that they are all from Yugoslavia. You see, it is always the problem if you did not do it exactly right from the beginning you sort of have to live with the next best, but the next best creates all sorts of new problems. I cannot help that. I can only test, we can only tell you we sort of applied the best test that is available at this late stage, but it has problems. It cannot be helped. It can never be a replacement for the test that I would have liked to have done before the trial started.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Is there a theoretical problem that witnesses or subjects who are tested think they might not distinguish between the ethnic background but in fact do? Is that an option?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure, if they tell you -- well, there is no problem because we cannot distinguish between those ethnic backgrounds anyway. That is what they say and many people can do things of which they are not aware at all. So, the answer is in the test, not in what they say about what the result of the test would be. You apply the test and then you know whether they can do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you find in your Belgrade research you did with this photospread any answer to this problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In our Belgrade research we found that they cannot distinguish between ethnic backgrounds, but there is this small proviso that I mentioned that is meaningful if we know that those pictures were representing people from the former Yugoslavia. Then it is really helpful, I think, that result and it sort of reassures us that the test, the photo test, was a fair test.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But as a matter of fact we do not know ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But there is a proviso.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As a matter of fact we do not know who those foils are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know that. I do not know about you. I do not know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Perhaps, your Honour, this is an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess until 2.30.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Professor Wagenaar, before the lunch break we had been discussing the ins and outs of the Doob and Kirshenbaum test and you did tell us about the uncertainties of the Prosecution photospread, did you not, when you referred to you do not know who the foils are, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the procedure that was followed when that photospread was used?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A little, at least not all that I would like to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We will go into that later. If you are not fully aware of the procedure that was followed when the Prosecution photospread was used and if you are not familiar with the identity and ethnic background of the foils, would such a photospread provide for a diagnostic, significant test?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, all I can say is that I cannot make a fair assessment of how diagnostic it is. If everything went according to the rules, it can be highly diagnostic and, in fact, say, an identification, identification evidence can rank among the best evidence that the Court can collect, if the procedures were right. If the procedures went wrong, it can be highly suggestive or even misleading and I cannot make a fair assessment of which is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So it simply comes down that we need to know more about these elements, procedure and who are they, to give any value to these test, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that is a fair conclusion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: In your letter of 10th October 1996 to the Defence, that is Exhibit D91, you described a number of weaknesses that threaten the reliability of the photospread. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you mention as a threatening factor earlier encounter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What does it mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means that if the witness encountered the accused or a picture of accused at any other time prior to the test, beside, say, possibly at the scene of the crime, then we do not know any longer what the identification means, whether it means that they met at the scene of the crime or not because the reason why now the witness recognises the accused could be the other encounter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Am I right in thinking that the probative value of the recognition also depends on the reliability of a witness claiming that he did not see the image of Mr. Tadic in newspapers or on television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure, if there is, in principle, a possibility that witnesses have seen images, say, on television or in newspapers ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was slow on that objection, but I am concerned about the intrusion of this witness's opinions into areas which are clearly the province of the Court; the assessment of reliability, the judgment of evidence. It is one thing to detail the factors based on his area of study which may in some manner reflect on that, but to begin making assessments of how the evidence interacts with that is, I think, beyond his camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I am not asking the witness, your Honour, to give an assessment on the reliability. I am simply asking him if the reliability of the witness is at stake, would that invalidate the test. That is all I ask. So is the reliability an issue which is relevant for the understanding and the value of the test.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Reliability ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: -- in terms of an answer of a witness to a question like having seen the image before on the TV.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: On the assumption that the witness is true when he says that he has not seen Dusko Tadic before, you may evaluate the test. I am simply asking, is it relevant then ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I will overrule the objection. I will overrule the objection. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. I will put the question again to you, Professor: am I right in thinking that the probative value of recognition depends on the reliability of the witness who claims that he did not know Mr. Tadic before the crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure, if in any case, if it is not certain, if, in principle, there has been an opportunity for seeing a picture of the witness, and it is not -- it cannot be established that the witness did not see such a picture, and the only thing you have is the witness's own statement about this, well, then the degree to which you trust that statement, of course, will affect your belief in the test.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is for the Court to decide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is for the Court to decide whether they want to trust that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is where we are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If the picture of Mr. Tadic was widely circulated, would that invalidate a recognition, even when the witness claims that he did not see the image of Mr. Tadic in newspapers or television because he is not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The same objection, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That seems to me that he is getting into telling the Judges how to make credibility assessments and -- well, that is what I feel. It may be that we decide not to accept a witness's statement when he says: "I have not seen Mr. Tadic on TV" when we know that his image has been broadcast widely since the trial began because of circumstances that we have learned from the witness, like lack of electricity in the area, that he is working certain shifts. We have heard witnesses regarding that. I really think that is a judgment for the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: May I rephrase the question then into is it possible then that the witness will claim he did not see anything but he is not aware of what he has seen? Is that in your field of expertise?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That sounds like a good question, because his training is in human perception and functioning of the memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He can tell us whether it is in the recess somewhere. OK. MR. WLADIMIROFF (To the witness): May I put the question to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is certainly possible that someone thinks he has not seen a certain picture whereas, in fact, he or she has.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Is there any research that will show how relevant this assumption might be in general or in specific cases?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, given the general possibility that this may happen to people, I think there is little else to say about how you apply that in a specific case, but it may have happened, such things may happen, and it is something I would say to evaluate, to be weighed by the Court, but there is nothing more you can say about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not a thing you can ask -- for instance, you can ask the

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: still have seen it?" because what could the witness say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Should it assist the Court in making the assessment on the value of such test if the Court was informed about the range and extent of the circulation of the picture of Mr. Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Dr. Wagenaar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There is an objection. I do not think this witness is an expert on this particular issue. He has already made his point that prior exposure may bear, in his view, on reliability. The factors which bear on what kind of exposure, the extent of exposure, are outside his province.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have no problem in withdrawing the question, your Honour. [To the witness]: Should it assist the Court to be informed about previous tests by other bodies than the Prosecution such as, for example, Bosnian and German authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think if there were previous tests with the same witnesses, if that is what you refer to, and there is a possibility that pictures of Mr. Tadic were shown on that occasion or on those occasions to the same witnesses, I think it would be highly relevant to know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to show this document for identification to the expert witness. I think that will be D93.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Show it to the Prosecution, but I think they have it in front of them, yes. Please familiarise yourself with what you have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have looked at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would you call this a photospread?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a collection of photographs. It could be used as a photospread.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Let me first ask you, do you speak German?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Does the top page of this document show that this is a collection of photos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, transparencies, I would say it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Does it also show on the top page that this map of photos is in a criminal case against Nikola Nikolic, Milenko Tomic, Dragan Vidic and a person called Zigic ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: --- who are accused of accessory to mass murder ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: ---- war crimes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Does this collection of photos show a photo of Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, photo No. 197, I would say, reminds me very much of the picture I have seen of him. I could be mistaken but .....

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Could you show that photograph on the overhead projector which is on your right side?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can we offer this -- would you offer it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, I will tender this document as D93, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there an objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, your Honour, there is not.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Defence 93 will be admitted. It is photo 197?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: This photo you see on your screen now is the photo you referred to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it has "197" on top.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I may refer to your letter of 27th March 1996, that is Exhibit D90, to the Prosecution. There is an attachment to that letter, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Could you show that attachment on the overhead projector, please, perhaps together with the other photo? Is there on that attachment a photograph of Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is No. 3, this one, as I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Am I unfair if I ask you whether that is the same photograph, the same image, according to your experience, seeing so many photos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I am not exactly certain it is the same photograph. I would argue that to me it looks very much like the same person. Whether it is exactly the same image, I am not certain of that. I have a better picture in my possession of No. 3 on the collection of photographs ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Before you do that, sir ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That I could show ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: --- let me first confer with the Prosecution. You got it from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Does the Prosecution object if I ask the witness to use the original that was given by you?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Specifically, no objection to the use of those photos. I think if it is an exhibit it should be made known to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: They should be exhibited. Before doing that I think it is fair enough to ask you because you were given them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I suppose I would also note that, perhaps, it is not necessary to display the photographs of these other individuals on television any longer than is necessary for purposes of the case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It would make it easier if I just use this photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I may -- excuse me, Professor -- Mr. Keegan suggests, I think perhaps prudently, that a redaction might be appropriate. We will try to find the time for the Court.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Now we are back to whether there is a better photograph of this image that is on the monitor. The question is what you have before you, is that the same photograph and, if so, put it on the monitor so that we can look at it. Do you want to mark that as 94?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, please, your Honour. Could you take that photograph of Dusko Tadic off ---

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Take it off the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: --- and put it on the Elmo, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is a little bit easier to compare because it is better quality and a bit larger. I would still find it (and it is not in my field of expertise) to say that two photographs are identical; it could well be the same photograph but since this is a photocopy with a lot of dark in it, which also always causes some changes, I would say it is not in my field of expertise to say that they are exactly the same photograph.
