I can just say that anybody could data the thing, that they look a lot the same. They do not say that as an expert in identification procedures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Would the showing to victims and witnesses from the former Yugoslavia of this German photospread in the criminal case against four suspects I have just mentioned invalidate the use of the Prosecution photospread in the Tadic case if used with the same witnesses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I should answer this question in a number of steps, if I may?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If in this photospread that contains this photo I had been made aware that this picture actually is the picture of a wanted person or of the accused so that I would remember this picture very well because I have spent more attention to it, then I think among the certain picture photospread that was used later, I think, it would be very easy to identify this particular photograph as representing the same person. That is the strongest case. A step less stronger is if I would just have seen the German photospread, not being aware which of the persons is the wanted person, so I would have, sort of, to remember all of the pictures, then there is still the possibility that seeing the second spread, the spread, the 13 picture spread, I would suddenly realise that one of these people I have seen before. That is a step less. The next step, still lesser step, is that after having seen this picture and being confronted with a certain picture photospread, I might not realise that I have seen one of them before and where I did, but still it may happen that one of these people looks more familiar than others, although I would not be aware of what the source of the familiarity is. Actually, although it seems to be the smaller step, the most remote from what would be endangering the procedure, that is the worst case, because now someone looks familiar and I do not know why, I cannot exclude that feeling because I realise it was from the previous test. So, in that situation the danger that I will now think I recognise that picture because I have seen this man, say, being involved in a crime instead of in another test, say, is the biggest. I am sorry for this long explanation, but the distinction is very important especially because, say, what apparently is the least case is, in fact, the worst.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Because it is in the recesses perhaps of your brain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It is familiar so you do not even realise that, in fact, you are making this connection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So a witness saying, "This man looks familiar" could be perfectly honest and still make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. The second threat you labelled in your letter was suggestion, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Suggestion" usually means in this context that there is something in the situation that guides the witness towards one of the pictures more than the others, and that something is not his memory to, say, a person who committed a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Does the procedure of the photo test play an important role here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, many elements of the correct procedures are exactly aimed at preventing various forms of suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court what these various forms might be?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance, a very simple one, if there is only one picture, then it is -- the suggestion is very strong that that must be the picture of a criminal. So a single person test is in itself highly suggestive. The instructions might in a strong form say, "I present you a series of photos. One of them is a criminal. Who do you think it is?" That suggested the criminal is there and that if you say, "Well, I do not recognise anyone", you would be wrong. Whereas, in fact, of course, the real situation is that if we apply the test we do not know whether one of them is a criminal or not. That is exactly what we want to find out. So the suggestion that there at least one of them is a criminal is highly suggestive. The instructions should clearly instruct, "Take care, maybe there is no one you recognise because we have the wrong person. Do not make just an identification at any cost. Do not guess. If you do not recognise it, just say it". That is a very important element of instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would it be advisable to avoid these kinds of suggestions to apply the test on the basis of written instructions given to the person who will execute the test?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure, well, if you are, as an investigator, highly experienced in this, you will be able to memorise the correct instructions and just say them without any written instruction in front of you. Usually, just to make sure that you do not forget anything, it is advisable to have the written instructions in front of you as an investigator and read them out to the witness. Another possibility is that you just present the written instructions to the witness and ask the witness to read the instruction him or herself. It is a little bit unnatural situation. Usually, what you have is a written instruction in front of you and you read it out to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would it be advisable to have an experienced investigator to do this, even though working with written instructions, or is it fair to say that if the instructions are correct and followed correctly does it matter whether he is experienced or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it would be advisable to have an experienced investigator because there are many pitfalls in this, apparently, so simple procedure, and you might make a number of mistakes even when you are totally unaware of what you are doing. So, the advantage of an experienced person is that he or she is aware of all that and would not make, say, just by accident such mistakes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would it be necessary to give each photo shown to the witness the same time of presentation to avoid suggestion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, and especially when or in the situation that the investigator knows which of the pictures represents the accused, because then, say, just even completely when the investigator is completely unaware of it, it is possible to treat that picture in a different way, present it longer or shorter or keep it under breath, or do anything that indicates that this picture is special.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would that be suggestive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That could be highly suggestive, yes. There is a quite a bit of research of, say, how small the clues need to be for a witness to pick them up and the result is very small.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would it be necessary to ask a witness to sign only at the back of one photo of the spread using fresh photos that have not been signed before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you need fresh photos, new photos for every witness, if you use the signing procedure, because if you turn the photo and this is the tenth witness and the witness perceives that there are nine signatures already on the back of the picture, then the witness becomes extremely confident that he or she got it right and will testify about recognition with greater confidence than the confidence that was felt during the recognition itself. So you gave that witness extra information that the witness cannot avoid to utilize; whereas, in fact, that information should not be available to the witness. The witness should not know whether the others also recognised him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The third threat you have mentioned in your letter of 10th October 1996 is capitalization of chance, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The set up of a photospread is such that it is, in principle, highly unlikely that a witness who is just guessing would guess right. Now, in some situations, say, that likelihood is increased and may be increased to an unwanted high level.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you notice any deviation in the image of the persons whose photographs have been used for the photospread, such as dark complexion or unshaven image?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are not exactly equal in a number of respects. I must say that it is very difficult to avoid also, but they do not all have the same complexion. One, as I described already in my letter to Mr. Tieger, is photographed against a slightly darker background which maybe the explanation why so many of my naive subjects identified that picture as representing a criminal. It sort of illustrates that if one sticks out for whatever reason, no matter how irrelevant that reason is, the darker background, subjects or witnesses may pick on that. It might be completely intuitive. There might be a reasoning behind it, like one is different, one is against a different background so the others came from the same, say, police file and the other was taken elsewhere or so ...... So, almost any clue that you give might be picked up. If it happens to detract from the accused, you cannot say that is unfair, but if it happens to point towards the accused, then it would be unfair. Indeed, there are slight differences with respect to how well they are shaven, how dark they are, they do not all have the same colour of hair. But I would say that there are enough, say, reasonable alternatives that look closely enough to the accused for me to not argue that the whole set up is clearly invalid.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You mentioned police file. Would it be relevant if a photospread contained photographs of persons whose photographs have been taken because of previous police contacts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in principle, there is nothing against taking photographs from a police file, but you should meet a number of conditions that I have mentioned before. One of them is that it should be absolutely certain that those persons have not been seen by the witnesses before, that they must not be from the same village or family members of the witnesses, and especially also they must not have been seen in war conditions in the former Yugoslavia. Now, these people, as far as I am aware, were photographed because they came into contact with the Dutch police. That is all that we know about them. We do not know where they came from, what their names are, whether they are family of the witnesses or whether after they were photographed in the Netherlands they returned to the former Yugoslavia and took part in war actions. There is nothing that we know about them, and it must be absolutely sure that that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you find in your letter you wrote about it the photospread test with witness Draguna Jaskic was repeated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I read those pages in the Court records. I found it very difficult to interpret what those actually said with respect to the procedure. What is suggested there is that she looked at the pictures, did not say she recognised anyone, and later on I get the impression that it was at a second meeting with the investigator, but I am not absolutely certain, she did mention to the investigator that, in fact, she had recognised anyone. I cannot infer from what is said, neither by her, neither by the investigator, what the actual procedure was, whether there were two meetings, whether there were two tests, one test at each meeting, what the reason for the second meeting was. I find that very unclear so I cannot really make a judgment of whether, say, an unwanted procedure has been used. But what I have written in my letter is her first reaction to the spread is clearly established. She said she did not recognise anyone and, according to proper rules, that would be the end of her testimony with respect to identification. You do not give people second chances, because you do not know what those mean, especially not, say, if there is a long delay between the two and the witness may have talked to I do not know how many people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You have read the statement of the investigator who did these tests. Do you remember how he did it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I do not have a copy of what he actually said in front of me, but from what he said I did not get a clear picture of the procedure that was used. Would it help if I mentioned a number of things that I would like to have known?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For instance, what I would like to have known is whether, say, the interview started with the photospread and then a discussion about experiences witnesses had eventually including, say, the person of Mr. Tadic, or whether there was first a discussion including Mr. Tadic and then the photospread. What you would like to know is if the photos were presented sequentially and I believe they were because they were in a booklet, not glued on one page as I have them but in a booklet with different pages, so you flick from one page to the other, what the exact procedure is. Let me give you an example: we have met a number of times. I assume that you are more or less familiar with my face. If there is a booklet with 13 pages in it and on one of the pages you find me, say, page 5, coming to page 5 you would say, "That's him". You did not -- you would probably not wait till page 15 and say, "Well, maybe there is a better Mr. Wagenaar at page 15". You would recognise me and say, "Hey, that is him", and there would be no need to go on beyond that page. If you would not completely recognise me and think, "Well, he looks a bit like him, but maybe there is a one -- in the following pages there is someone who looks a bit more like him even", then you are making a different type of judgment. You are not judging whether you recognise a person; you are judging who looks most like a certain person without making the assessment of whether it is him or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Is that the reason why a protocol would be required of the test?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So what you would want is, in the least, a protocol: When did the witness say, "I recognise that person", at the end or as soon as he or she saw the page? And what happened afterwards? Was it allowed, for instance, to go back? Was it allowed to go all the way to page 15 and then say, "Well, I think No. 3 looked most like him", or was the rule as soon as you have passed page 3 you cannot name No. 3 any more because you should have done it when looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You should have been told that before the test is run?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, that would be a reasonable rule. I would, at least, want to know what was the rule and then we can form a judgment about is that a reasonable rule or not. Another rule applies too

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: is what if the person says, if the witness says, looking at page 2, "Ah, that person I recognise". Remember the question was only, "Is there anyone you recognise?", not "Do you recognise Mr. Tadic?" as far as I am aware of. So what would happen if a witness said: "Well I recognise No. 2", would the investigator go on presenting the other pictures, because that means that, in fact, you get a number of shots. The more shots you get, the more likely it is that you recognise someone. Or would the investigator stop immediately after, say, a first identification has been made and say, "Stop, that is it. I will not show you the other pictures"? Remember, the more recognitions you make, say, the more shots you have had, and the larger likelihood that one of the shots is a hit. Now, the investigator knowing, say, who the accused is, might simply say, discount, say, the false identifications and accept the correct ones. So you need a clear rule for that. I assume that nothing might have gone wrong. I can only state I cannot see in the various statements that have been made what the exact rules in the procedure were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would it be relevant for the witness doing the test to know that the investigator is coming from the International Tribunal in the case against Dusko Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well, at least if the witness knows that the investigator came to investigate the case of Tadic, then of course the suggestion that the photospread is shown in order to identify Mr. Tadic might be present, this will be stronger after you have discussed Mr. Tadic for a certain period of time. In fact, it would not even be so bad. The best case would be if, say, the question was clearly, "We have talked about a Mr. Tadic, now I am going to show you a picture. I will ask you, say, whether Mr. Tadic is among these pictures". Then the situation is perfectly clear to the subject. There is no uncertainty about what the objective is. Now if you only ask, "Is there someone you recognise?" the problem is that the witness may point at various people and you cannot even say that the witness is wrong because it is quite possible that the witness recognises No. 2 or No. 8 because they are from the same village. So, you would, logically, have to allow a number of responses, positive responses, to the witness, because it can happen that those are correct responses, but it is exactly what you do not want because three or four response means three shots.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Returning to the test with Draguna Jaskic and the investigator who run that test twice, would you describe the involvement of that investigator as being a professional performance of the test, a proper performance of the test?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Objection. Again, that may be more a matter of the way the question is phrased or framed, but I think the question should be -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You said a "proper involvement". Why do you not ask the witness whether it meets professionally accepted standards in his field as opposed to our field.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes, I will, your Honour. I will withdraw the question. [To the witness]: How would you describe the quality of the test run by that investigator?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is very hard for me to make an assessment because I have no clear impression of what happened. What disturbs me a little bit is that there is no clear description of what happened. I would say the least you can expect of a professional investigator is a very clear description that leaves no question marks with respect to important matters of procedure. I can really cannot make a proper assessment of what happened or, say, whether important rules were violated or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Professor, from your CV it appears that you wrote a lot about the procedural aspects of these kinds of tests, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I do not know what you call "a lot", but I published about it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to show this document to the witness for identification. That will be D6 -- I have lost which number it will be, your Honour -- 94, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It should be 95. The picture of Mr. Tadic will be 94. It has been marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should take this opportunity to note the redaction points, that would be 14.55.30 to 14.57.20, the video portion.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think it has been done.

utterances.speaker: MISS FEATHERSTONE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: If we are talking about the correct times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Professor, is this a photocopy of chapter 3 of your book identifying even a case study in legal psychology published in 1988?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So it seems, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender this document as D95.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Defence 95?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Defence 95 will be admitted. Are you going to offer 94?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If I did not I offer it, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Any objection to Defence 94, the photo of Mr. Tadic that was taken from Dr. Wagenaar's records?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Professor, if I may discuss with you some of the rules of that chapter? If we look to the first rule, and perhaps I should give the Court copies. What I intend to do, Professor, is to go through the rules, those rules which might be relevant for this case, and just to wrap up all the issues we have discussed so far. Rule 1: Can an involvement in a crime be proved by means of a lineup or a show up when the suspect is known to the witness for other reasons than involvement in the crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we have discussed this before. Such a test would not logically place the witness at the scene of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Should identification of a suspect not known to the witness for other reasons than encounter during the crime be achieved by means of a lineup and not a show up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, by a "show up" in this rule I mean a one person test, and a one person test is not a difficult test to pass and it does not show that you really recognise this person; you only have to say "yes".

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you find any one person test in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not with the four witnesses that I would think are really relevant as identification subjects. They were all multi-person tests.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you find any two photo tests?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not with those four. Two photo tests were used for some of the other 48 ones, but as long as, say, the purpose of those tests is only to verify, say, that there is no mistake about the person and not the objective to logically place the accused at the scene of the crime, I have no objection against those two person tests.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Is the selection of a suspect through mug file inspection acceptable as proof of identify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "Mug file inspections" usually mean a collection of pictures that are shown to a victim of a crime in order to find a suspect, not to recognise a suspect, but to first find during the investigation, say, the identity of a possible suspect. Those mug files are not selected on the basis of, say, the description or a detailed description and, therefore, cannot pass as a fair lineup or identity parade. Therefore, mug file inspections can be used for investigations, not as proof of identity. They are two different things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Have you found any mug file inspection in this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no. There is one problem, though, that, as I mentioned before, in a real identity parade, either, say, live or photographic, you would completely know who the foils are and that they are innocent, and we do not that right now. So there is a slight problem that, say, the nature of the spread that was used cannot be defined exactly, but I would not qualify it as just a simple mug file inspection because clearly it is not. It is better than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. I jump to rule 7 now. Should the witness be asked to identify the same suspect more than once?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because if you show, say, the same suspect twice, that is suggestive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If I may jump to Rule 10 then, when there are more witnesses available, should a falsification of an initial identification be attempted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in principle, when you have many witnesses, it is a good procedure to ask them all to identify the accused person. The reason is that is related to what we discussed before. You should, of course, never hide negative outcomes of identification tests, but you should also make -- give yourself the opportunity to get negative results. For instance -- but I must apologise because scientists always make these hypothetical cases and create problems thereby -- imagine that there are 10 witnesses and they just guess. One of them guesses correct. That might be the first one. If you now stop, you do not ask the other ones, you will never know that it was a guess. You have to ask them, all 10, and then you will find out that the others do not recognise them. So in order -- we would say you must -- you make yourself vulnerable after initial successes and be sure that it was not just a guess. That is why you should ask all witnesses to identify if they have seen the accused or if they have seen, no, the perpetrator. Right? If they have not seen anything that is relevant, they cannot make an identification. But if, in principle, they would be good identification witnesses, you should also use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may proceed to rule 11 then: Should all identification attempts, whether successful or not, be reported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I think we have discussed that and the reason why is quite clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right. Would this include also witnesses who have not been called to testify in Court but who were interviewed during discovery, that is, pretrial stage but not called in Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in principle, I think every test that has been applied during the investigation process ought to be reported and made known to the Court, because if you do not do that, and of course I do not want to suspect anybody of bad intentions, but it would be possible, in principle, to hide the negative ones and propose the positives ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If I proceed to rule 12 then: Should reports about identification attempts with negative results provide all available information that could help to understand the value?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very clearly, and a negative result may be completely uninteresting if we know that, in fact, the witness was an onlooker from 300 metres distance. Of course, that would be very difficult to identify. It does not mean the accused is not the wanted person. If the witness, on the contrary, was at a distance of one and a half metres and has watched on for several hours and he would be unable to identify the accused, that is highly informative because that suggests that possibly the accused is the wrong person. So you would want -- even the negative outcomes can highly informative, and can only be interpreted if you know, say, the conditions in which they occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did the procedure that was applied to the witness we just discussed, that lady witness we just discussed, meet this rule?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is very difficult for me to say that because, as you realise, I only received a limited number of pages relating to her testimony. So I am not completely sure about how much about that case is known to the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The Court has seen the same pages and heard the same evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I have not seen her complete testimony, I think, so I do not want to express opinions or judgments about things that maybe are different when I would have looked at the complete transcript of her testimony here in Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At least I can say that from the pages I have read what has happened is not clear to me, and I would have liked a clear description of what she has seen initially, whether she would be able to identify him easily and what has happened during, say, the test and the second encounter that, apparently, has occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If I now may proceed to rule 13: Will the probative value of an initial identification be increased through identification by other eyewitnesses, the number of the identifications?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The general idea of that rule is that, say, there is no linear relationship between the number of witnesses who identify and the amount of, say, trust that the Court should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me give you an example: if an accused has a twin brother who looks exactly like him, then it is quite possible that the first witness will be mistaken there and also quite likely that all the others will be mistaken in the same way. So you cannot then say, "Ah, but because now we have 20 witnesses it cannot be the twin brother". So, the sheer number of witnesses is not, say, the most relevant piece of information. For that reason, I would say, if I may refer to the present case, four witnesses, although compared to the 50, the 48 others may look a small number, in view of this rule, it would not be so extremely useful to find more than four who identify. If the procedure is correct and you can trust those identifications, I would say that is quite enough. Do not go for also another 48 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. If I proceed to rule 14: Should investigators do everything within their power to prevent contacts among witnesses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and on purpose this is formulated in this way to do everything within your power because it is not -- usually not within our power to prevent all contacts among witnesses. If they are father and son or wife and husband, then that simply cannot be avoided, especially not when the time between the crime and the appearance in Court is very long. Then, of course, it may happen that witnesses exchange information about the identity of possible perpetrators. But I think investigators should not aggravate that problem by adding, say, their own contacts when it can be avoided. There are a number of examples in cases where the investigation itself is the reason why witnesses came into contact with one another and that, I think, should be avoided.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would it be relevant then that more than one member of the same family is asked to participate in the photospread test?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, indeed, if it were possible to find witnesses who have not been in contact with one another, that would be much better than to get all witnesses from the same family. So if you want to choose four, it would be better to choose four totally independent ones than family members. If it is established that they are family members and have been in contact, say, during a long period and have discussed the case and identity of perpetrators and so on, then of course it is quite possible, generally speaking, that information about, say, the appearance of a perpetrator is transferred from one person to the other. Things about, well, the name itself might be highly suggestive because if one did not recognise someone but the other did and the first witness says, "Well, did you not recognise so and so?" that may stick, of course, and the image then may be formed and then the later recognition might follow. The beauty, of course, of, say, the multiple person identity parade is that if the parade is organised well, it would be very difficult to transfer information that would help you to get at the correct choice. It will especially help you if the parade is not well organised. So that, for instance, if you say, "Well, he had dark hair", and there is only one with dark hair in the spread, then such information might help. In a good spread they would all have dark hair and it would not have helped. So that is something that maybe is important to notice. Some violations are not so bad in an isolated situation. They may become terribly bad in combination with one another. So this one, contacts among witnesses, and a not so well chosen set of pictures in combination may make it suddenly extremely easy for witnesses who do not remember the appearance of the perpetrator to get at the right picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. If I may proceed to rule 15: Should investigators ask witnesses before the identification attempt whether or not they discussed the case with other people and should they not record such questions and answers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think in connection with the previous rule it is clear why, at least, you would want to know about it. Then you can later make decisions, say, how much weight you want to attach to certain witnesses on the basis of that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Rule 16: Should witnesses be excluded from an identification test if it is established that they could base their identification partly or wholly on information transmitted by other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think if you have a situation where you know that it is possible that the witness received information that might with some degree of certainty enable this witness to identify this one picture, I think in that case you should exclude the identification of such a witness because it might be misleading.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Rule 17: Should witnesses before participation in an identification test be requested to provide a verbal description of the criminal as they remember him and should that description be included in the reports of the subsequent identity test?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the idea of an identity test is that the witness has somewhere in memory a more or less circumscribed representation of the perpetrator, some image that can be used for a later recognition. One can ask the witness to describe that image. It might be more or less vague, but the witness must be able to describe what it is. Is that an image of a man or of a woman? Is it a dark person or a fair person? Is it a tall or a small person? All sorts of questions that the witness, in principle, must be able to answer. Let me give you an example: if the witness cannot say whether it was a man or a woman, then I would say then a very precise identity parade would not help very much, and it would not be indicated to apply then a further test if the rough image is not present. It is possible that the person has a -- the witness has a rather clear image, but that image differs completely from the appearance of the accused. For instance, if the witness says, "Well, it was a man fitting that description" but the accused is a woman, I would be very hesitant to go on with further identity tests because there is a conflict there. Probably the witness remembers someone, refers to someone else and then it is suggestive to go on with a person who does not even fit this rough description. If I may give you another example, the situation I have been in? The suspect is a very tall black person, but the accused is a rather small fair haired person. So, in order to make a fair test you have a number of fair people -- they all fit the same description as the accused -- and now you have to ask the witness: "Who of these small fair people is the tall black person you remember?" That would be a, sort of, very difficult situation to handle for the witness and should, therefore, be avoided.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. You have answered in the meantime rule 18, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I ask you a question? Is it not possible, though, for the memory to be blocked by the occurrence, so that being shown a picture as opposed to being asked to describe, when it has been blocked because of the very violence, perhaps, if it was a violent occurrence, that it would be better to be shown a picture rather than to be asked, and to be asked to give the description when it has been blocked and not be allowed to go forward with a picture would defeat the purpose, would it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure, sure, your Honour. That would be perfectly possible. The question is whether such a witness would be a good identification witness, and the situation I have described to you, sort of, illustrates the problem. If you cannot use the initial description of the witness to, sort of, select what the lineup should look like, you may confront the witness with a lineup that simply poses logical problems to this subject. Indeed, you are right; there might be a subject who suddenly realises, "Ah, ha, I was totally wrong and now I see who did it and I recognise this person". But there might be other subjects who are totally confused and start to guess or show other types of behaviour that is misleading. So, generally, you would want to avoid that situation. So, although, and I agree, in the later rules you will also see that sometimes it is necessary to violate these rules, sometimes the conditions simply do not allow you to stick to all the rules and still you want to solve a case and provide the evidence. Of course, when there is a good reason for it and you can justify why you violated the rules, at least a Court can consider that. So it is not by necessity and automatically that the violation of the rule should lead to a rejection of the evidence. But I think, as long as there is no reason not to follow the rules, it is wise to stick to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If I proceed to rule 19, Professor: Should the witness be instructed to identify only one person, that is the person he described, prior to the test?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in principle, the situation is if there are a number of people in front of you, if you recognise, say, the person you are asked to identify, there can be only one of them, and you cannot fire twice because that simply doubles the likelihood that you will have a hit. So you should indicate either none or one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That should be told to the ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And that should be told to the witness because it happens sometimes that witnesses are so quick that before you know it they have named two persons, and then what should you do?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I take it, according to rule 20, that those instructions should be recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in order to be certain that the proper instructions were given, it would be very nice to simply have them in the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Dealing with these reports, does rule 20 have anything to do with the matter of certainty, for example, if different investigators run tests?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well, there is always the problem if you are afterwards asking an investigator whether there is one or many, how did you do it, you rely on their memory. I would say it is bad enough that you have to rely on the memory of witnesses, but that cannot be avoided. You should not complicate that by also having to rely on the memory of investigators which can be avoided. Now, the problem is, of course, if you have many investigators, if they have not agreed about a certain procedure, then the likelihood increases that they will have you different procedures, in fact, but the question is whether you will ever find out if they have not made a record of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It is a problem, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It should not be a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If I may proceed to rule 21? Should the instruction to the witness stress that the wanted person is possibly not in the parade or in the photospread and that, therefore, a positive response should be made only when the witness is certain of recognising that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is highly important that you tell the witness not to make an identification if the witness is not certain, because it is quite possible that there is no one here she can recognise. The research on, say, the presence or absence in instruction of that piece, in fact, is reported in the chapter that precedes this chapter, and that shows that it has, I would call it, a very large effect on the false positives on the identification of foils.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Could I just request the question? I see the word "mug shot" is used here again. What is your definition of a "mug shot" as distinct from a simple photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Usually, mug shots or a mug shot collection is used as simply a number of photos from the police files, often with numbers on them but not necessarily, and there can be a large number. I say the largest number that I have seen being used was over 500. These mug shots are usually selected on the basis of a very, very superficial description of a perpetrator, and are selected in order to find the identity of a suspect. So, you do not have a suspect yet, there is no one you suspect but you try to find the identity of a suspect; whereas a photospread is constructed after you have a suspect because the suspect is one of them and the others (and usually not 500 but five to 10, say, would be quite enough) are selected especially in such a way that they resemble this one suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So that a mug shot is not a characteristic of a particular photograph, but rather of the time and ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: --- make up of the collection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible that, say, one picture appears in a mug shot and another time it appears in a proper photospread, but then it has been selected for that particular purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Looking to rule 22, Professor, I think you have answered or you have responded to that rule, that is, should police officers in charge of identification procedures have received the appropriate training and should they be able to demonstrate their professional qualifications both in written and oral testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and the reason is that the procedures are, in fact, so much more difficult than you would think it is that you need training to do it, to do it right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If I may proceed to rule 28? Should all foils of an identity test fit the prior description obtained from witnesses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, if it does not, if they do not, then those foils might be easily discarded by the witness which makes the probability of just guessing who the accused is higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If I may proceed to Rule 29? Can prior descriptions of the criminal that do not fit the suspect's appearance be used on the selection of foils? I think you answered to that rule too, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but I think that must be qualified because the question is, of course, what discrepancies are acceptable and what are not. What is really meant by rule 29 is that gross discrepancies, say, calling a man a woman or calling a white person a Japanese person or calling a very tall person a small person. That would qualify for some sort of dismissal of the situation. What does not qualify, for instance, is the absence or presence of a moustache, a beard, or things like that because they are considered to be minor things. Also, matters of length, age, weight, should be accepted with very wide margins because these things are not easily to perceive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you did address that matter in your letter of 10th October, Exhibit 91, that is, your letter to the Defence. You also gave an opinion on the problem of facial hair. Could you tell the Court what is the relevance of that problem or is this a relevancy at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I took the freedom to comment on that because I saw it discussed so many times in the records and I thought, since apparently it is a problem to others, I should say something about it. The situation appears to be, as I understood it, that sometimes Mr. Tadic had facial hair growth and sometimes he had not. He was completely clean shaven or had a full beard and sometimes also he was badly shaven. Now, I would say to those who have known him for a long time that would be no obstacle at all to recognise him in any condition because they have seen him in all conditions. You might in a way say they have in their memory they have pictures of him in all various conditions and, no matter what he looks like now, they would always be able to recognise him. For those who did not know him, the question is a little bit more complicated, because if they have seen a person committing a crime who was, say, clean shaven, just to give an example, now they see an accused who has a full beard, you would, in principle, be asking them to see through the beard and, sort of, guess what this person would look like, say, without the beard. Sometimes it was suggested that for that reason accused people shave off their beards or let their beards grow. But I would say the beauty of a well organised identity test is that it solves that problem. If, say, the picture shown to them has the wrong facial hair growth and they can still recognise him, they recognise him, and it cannot be guessing because the set up is so that guessing would not help them. If they cannot recognise them, they do not recognise them, period, then you have to ask, why do they not recognise them? One of the explanations could be it is the hair growth. But if they recognise them, then obviously the hair growth did not pose a problem. So, logically, I would say for the large group of witnesses who knew him hair growth can hardly be of any relevance, and for those who did not know him, these four, well, we had to test to see whether it posed a problem and, as much as we can trust the test, the result is it did not pose a problem. That is the beauty of such a test.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If well performed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If well performed, of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Talking about recognition and facial hair, what would be an appropriate distance for a live recognition in daytime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have published on that, I am not sure -- no, that is not in the list of literature I offered to you at the end of the letter of 10th October. I have a rather extensive publication on problems of distance and lighting conditions with respect to the recognition of faces, where it says that in daylight at a distance of more than 15 metres problems start. If there is a possibility that, say, two people look, are a bit similar, then from a distance of 15 metres the general, average observers start to make mistakes. I am not saying that at 15 metres you cannot recognise a person, but that is about where problems start, 15 metres. Less than 15 metres, I would say there is no problem. You would see whether that is the one individual that you know or not. Beyond 15 metres, that is the shortest distance at which problems start, and then, of course, the problems increase the longer the distance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Within 15 metres would facial hair be a problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not -- it depends again. We have to distinguish between these two groups. The group who knew him already before with facial hair might not have had a problem because that is the face they were used to. Those who did not know him and saw him for the first time there and then with the beard, initially there is no problem. They do not recognise anything at that time because that is their first perception of that person. Only later there is a problem, there might be a problem, because if the test presents someone without the facial hair, then they may not recognise him, but again the test solves that problem. That is the beauty of it. If the perception was not good enough initially, they will not recognise him, they will fail the test, and then we know it. If they recognised him in the test, apparently the perception was good enough. That is what the test proves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: So if the basis is all right, that is, within 15 metres ----

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: --- if the basis is all right, then the story is valid as has been discussed today running a proper test?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, no, maybe I have to correct you there. Even if they saw the perpetrator at a longer distance, it is quite possible that they saw him correctly and accurately, we can know that from the later test. That is what the test is for. If they did not perceive him correctly, they will fail the later test. The test is to show that their original perception was accurate enough, and in this situation you are now in, provided there are no doubts about the quality of the test, those four tests show that there were not these perception problems. But you have to be certain that there is no problem in the test. But if there is no problem, the beauty of the design of the test is that now you can be certain the perception was accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I think this is an appropriate moment, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. Professor, we were left before the break with the issue of prior descriptions. If we proceed to rule 30, should an identity test be interpreted with the requisite prudence when there is not at least one prior description that fits the suspect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and the reason is that, ideally, you would select foils in an identity test on the basis of the description that has been given by witnesses. If you cannot do that, then possibly the test is less appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. If we now proceed to rule 31, we spoke about the foils that had been used by the Prosecution photospread. Rule 31 says that members of an homogenous group such as police should normally not be used as participants in an identification parade. Would that also apply to foils who are not from the same profession but from an ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, in principle, first, the danger is that if you select foils from one homogenous group, then in one way or the other the accused might stick out. If you want to avoid that, you do not choose the foils from one homogenous group. But you can also test whether something has gone wrong by applying the Doob & Kirschenbaum test. That we have done to this particular material and the results do not suggest that something has gone wrong there, but we do not know exactly, as I mentioned before, who the foils are, but I have no particular reason here to suspect that on the basis of a violation of this rule something has gone terribly wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If we now proceed to rule 32: "Should foils be selected such that others who have been witnesses to the crime will find no clues that help -----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: "Have not been".

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: "Who have not been" -- you are perfectly right, your Honour, thank you -- have not been witnesses to the crime will find no clues that help him to guess who is the suspect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well, in fact, that rule is a formulation of the Doob & Kirshenbaum test. Ideally, you would apply that before you show the test to any witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If I may jump to rule 34? Should the actual material used for a photo identification test be kept for later inspection and should automatically be given to the Defence, and should the record reflect the order in which photos were shown or the arrangement of the photos as they were shown?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because in order to interpret the test or to give it the proper weight, you should exactly know what has been shown in which manner. The rule mentions the Defence. It is implied, of course, that is also presented to the Court because finally it is the Court who has to give the proper weight to the test.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Is it your finding that this rule was obeyed in this case, as far as you could read from the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well -----

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour, that is way beyond the scope of this witness's expertise. As a matter of fact ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Why is it beyond his expertise in terms of the arrangement of the foils and what was done in this case? We have in evidence the photospreads that were shown to the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Did you see them?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As I understand the question, this witness is being asked to determine from the transcript and the materials provided to him a factual matter, not provide an expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I thought the matter that he was asked -- maybe I missed the question then -- was whether rule 34 -- I guess you are right then. It relates back to the previous rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The problem may lie in the underlying question, that is, requesting this witness to offer an opinion about rules of procedure is a different matter from asking him what factors may or not affect the reliability of an identification. Those are matters both for the Court to determine factually and to be applied to the rules of the Court. He is not here as a consultant on how the Tribunal should proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It is listed as a rule and you are challenging the appropriateness of it being included as a rule when it has nothing to do with whether the identification procedures are proper, but instead whether they were given to opposing counsel and the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think, in fact, the presence of this particular rule which is irrelevant to the matters for which this witness was called in the body of these rules do, in fact, indicate that these rules or stated rules go beyond his stated area of expertise and into the province of determining procedures, making recommendations, having a wish list and so on. But focusing on this particular so-called rule, it is clearly not a matter for this witness and not within his stated expertise. I can understand how a person involved in this work might come to certain opinions. He can offer them in other forms if he wishes, but it is not relevant here.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I have no problem in withdrawing the question, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. If I may proceed to rule 36? Should names and addresses of participants in the parade be recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and the reason for that is given in this chapter. Sometimes it is necessary to repeat a line up or get a clear impression of a line up, and then you should be able to get in touch with those people who appeared in the parade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That would enable the parties in the trial to assess whether the criteria were met as described in these rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the present situation where we have a photographic line up, it is less relevant, I think, because all the material that has been shown to witnesses is available. You do not need the names and addresses of, say, the witnesses in order to recreate the test situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If I may proceed to Rule 39? Should transformations occurring in the period between the crime and the identification test be counteracted as much as possible?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but the rule clearly says "as much as possible" because it is not always possible. So, if you talk about, say, a long delay like 10, 20 or 30 years, clearly the accused looks older and that cannot be corrected any more. The advantage of a photographic lineup is exactly in this, that you may obtain a picture of the accused, say, taken in the time that the crime took place, so that there is a -- there might be the closest possible resemblance between that picture and what the witnesses saw in case they saw the accused which has to be established, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you find any indication when a photo of Mr. Tadic was taken that was a part of the photospread?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that, no, but if it had been possible to find a picture that was taken in that time, that would be a clear advantage of using the photo test in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Rule 40: Should identification tests, whenever it is possible, be administered by police officers who do not know which person in the lineup is the suspect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and the reason I think we have already also discussed. The reason is that it is possible totally without any conscious of it to give hints or clues at the witness that, sort of, give away the identity of who is the accused in the lineup.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Could you give us an example?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Like, say, with the showing of photographs, a slightly longer presentation, or the keeping of the breath, a hesitation when the subject responds to a foil. There are many ways in which that can happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Rule 41: Should the presentation of photographs be strictly limited to a preset time period, and should the witness be informed about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, one reason is that if you allow a variation in presentation time, that is a way in which witnesses can be influenced; and the other is that if we talk about a proper recognition, then that happens within a rather short time. You do not need hours to recognise someone whom you remember very well. So if you make the presentation time or the response time too long, you sort of invite all sorts of guessing that you would not get if you restricted it to a short period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Rule 42: Should all relevant details of the preparation and the conduct of the identification test be recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because to the Court it is extremely important to give the proper weight to identification tests on the basis of, say, the appropriateness of the procedures that have been followed. In order to do that, you have to know what procedures have been followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Rule 43: Should a witness be given feedback with respect to whether they identified a suspect or a foil?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, witnesses should not be given feedback because usually the identification takes place out of Court. The witness has to testify later in Court about that and may misremember the confidence at the time of the recognition, because if they have given the feedback that this, indeed, was the accused, they may increase their confidence and exhibit this confidence in court which sort of suggests that the identification was made with that same confidence which is not necessarily true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Rule 44: Is there any diagnostic reason to give Defence counsel the right to attend identification tests?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well, there are many reasons to do that. One is that for the whole investigation it is much more useful for anybody to detect any wrong procedures before you hold the test than afterwards. After you have held the test you cannot do it again and you might have lost a witness. If you find out before you hold the test that is something is wrong you can correct it, and so all parties -- since all parties, in principle, profit from, say, an accurate test because it leads you close to the truth, it would be very relevant to ask the Defence to canvass a critique prior to the test, not afterwards. I must say not all Defence counsel agree with me because many seem to like just to give the criticism afterwards instead of, sort of, making it optimal before.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I appreciate that. If we may proceed to Rule 45? Should identifications be accepted as evidence when witnesses declare to see only a resemblance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think the question of identification test is to establish identity, and identity means the sameness of the person whom you saw commit a crime and the person in front of you, not the resemblance but the sameness. So just establishing resemblance is not good enough. That does not count as an identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Does it mean that the officer who is performing the test should be instructed not to accept a resemblance as a positive identification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would say let the officer exactly report what has been said. If a witness says, "I see a resemblance", that is what should be reported. Then you can leave it to the Court to decide whether that should be accepted as an identification or not. In my opinion, it should be not, but if it is just presented to the Court as an identification without, say, the full detail of it, then you have taken away the Court's ability to make that decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Rule 46: Should full recognitions pronounced only after a considerable time be accepted as a positive identification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, well, as I said, a recognition is something that comes immediate to you and not after weeks or many hours. So when a witness cannot, say, immediately state a full recognition, then you should count it as a non-recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: 47: Should other expressions or uncertainties on the part of the witness be recorded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and there are all sorts of expressions of uncertainty that may happen in practice, like I think it is No. 3 but it might also be No. 7, if you record it as a full recognition of No. 3, well, that statement would not reflect the actual, say, quality of the recognition. There are many expressions of uncertainty that witnesses express and, yes, they should be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Again to allow the Court to make a full assessment of what is the quality of the test, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If I may proceed to Rule 48? Why is it that dock identifications never can be accepted as proof of identity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is extremely easy for any person, whether he or she has any knowledge of any remembrance of the perpetrator, to point at someone who is in the dock in the courtroom. It is hard to imagine that someone would fail to realise who the accused is in the courtroom. So the probative value of that cannot be very high because it is not a difficult test to pass. The general rule is the more difficult the test, if you pass it, it means more. This is an extremely easy test so it can hardly mean anything at all. If there is a question whether the witness has any remembrance of what the perpetrator looks like, if that is really a question, then you should test it in a proper test, not in a test that anyone can pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If I may proceed to rule 49? Should a breach of rules, as we have been discussing so far, when not justified in a written report, lead to a rejection of an identification in terms of quality of your field of expertise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There I might be invading, say, what is called the domain of the Court, I think, because it is not for me to reject any tests. So I know that rule is maybe not appropriate for an expert to express, but of course it contains a clear warning that there are cases in which rules were being breached to such an extent that really the logical impact of the recognition is totally absent. In that case at least I think it should be made known to the Court that there is a real problem. I do not want to express here that I would prescribe, want to prescribe, to the Court what to decide in such a case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That might apply to rule 52 ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: --- I believe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course, the rule is not based upon nothing. Of course, the rule is based upon what is written above. At that time it was just a comment in the Devlin Report that was published in the United Kingdom. In the meantime, that has been adopted in the code there and is a rule. So I am not just making up my own rules. I know that in some countries that is a rule, and I do not think it is a bad rule, but it is not for me now to form, create, any opinion on that for this Court. This Court has its own rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: May I just ask one question? Is that what you meant, Dr. Wagenaar, when you very early in your testimony said that if it can be shown that there are gross violations of procedures for the four people who we are talking about now, then the test would not be valid? 50 does speak in terms of whether it should be accepted, but certainly (and maybe that is our province) you can testify as to whether an identification procedure is proper, is that not so, or valid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: As I recall your testimony, you said if there are really gross violations of procedures for the four, then it would not be valid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Is that not what 50 is talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: OK. Did you find any gross violations of the procedure used for the four people here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I lack a lot of information. There are a number of aspects on which I have simply no opinion because I do not have the information. I can only notify to you that, say, the information could not be found in the record, but there is hardly any positive information in the record that indicates that rules have been breached. I think you can also find that in my letter dated 10th October that my problem is mainly absent -- lack of information than the positive indication that rules have been breached.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Everything that you have been talking about with respect to these rules here, these 50 rules, they relate to the four people who did not know Mr. Tadic but the photographic test was used for identification purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Not recognition, identification purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, right. So if those four witnesses would not have appeared in the record, I think we could have just prevented this whole discussion about identification problems because it particularly focuses on those four.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: OK. Very good. Excuse me, Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): You did not find any breach or violation of these rules because there was no information there, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, there are some slight problems that I notified. They are not immediately, say, identifiable as gross breaches of procedure. But, for instance, the thing that I have mentioned, the instruction to the witnesses is not perfectly clear to me because it was not given in detail. What I read in the record gives a very short instruction to the witnesses, saying something to the extent of, "Is there anyone in this spread that you recognise?" If that is all, if the other things that ought to be present in the instructions, in fact, were absent, then I would say that is problematic, but I have no full knowledge of the instructions so I can only point the Court to say that lack of information that there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Did you find that the rules were obeyed or is there no information about that too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say there is not enough information for me to form an opinion about whether, say, the proper rules were followed wherever it was possible. But again I want to stress that I realise very much that in some conditions you simply cannot follow all rules; you can just do the best that you can and, well, that should be good enough to present in Court and then it is up to the Court to decide whether, say, the logic of the whole test is still acceptable. But I cannot form an opinion on that because in the selection from the record that I have seen there is not much information about the procedures that were followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What I will try to do now is to list with you what will be helpful for the Court to know in order to make a reasonable assessment about the quality of the test. Would it be helpful for the Court if the Court knows whether witnesses have been asked to identify the suspect more than once, either by the Prosecution or by any other authority such as the German authorities or the Bosnian authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, definitely. We are talking about the four subjects? Yes, I think that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would it be helpful for the Court to have all identification attempts using the photospread, whether successful or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. You mean of these witnesses or other witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: All witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All attempts?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: All attempts known to either party in this trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure. I think that the weight of these identifications cannot be determined without knowing how many other tests there were and how many of them were successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would it be helpful for the Court to have information about the instructions that were given to the investigators performing the tests?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in as much as these instructions can give the Court insight into the procedures that were used, because I think the exact procedures should have been in instructions to the investigators, because otherwise there is no guarantee that they would all apply the same procedures. To that extent, I think it would be very useful to know those instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would it be helpful for the Court to know whether the witnesses have been asked before the identification attempt whether or not they discussed the case with other people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in as far as these other people could have informed them about the outer appearance of the accused or the perpetrator, which is not necessarily the same, it would be important to know what they have learned about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would it be helpful for the Court to know whether the witnesses before participation in an identification test have been requested to provide a verbal description of the person they later identified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would even go further. I think it would be very important to know what these descriptions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Should these descriptions, if any available, be produced to assist the Court in this matter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure, because I think it would be extremely informative if, say, those descriptions do not coincide with the outer appearance of your client, well, or do coincide, that would also be very useful. It would be very useful in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would it be helpful for the Court to know whether witnesses were instructed to identify only one person, that is, the person who fits the specific verbal description which was produced by that same witness prior to the test?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that because that is the proper question to ask, "Identify this one person", and not just anybody, because in the given condition they might correctly recognise more than one person, because they might have been familiar with some of the foils that would lead them to, say, multiple responses which again increases the probability of guessing correctly. So that is something that should have been, sort of, shielded off by the instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would it be helpful for the Court to know whether the witnesses have been instructed that the wanted person is possibly not in the photospread and that, therefore, a positive response should be made only when the witness is certain of recognising that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because that is an essential element in the instructions to subject and I think the Court ought to be certain that it was said in this manner to the witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would it be helpful for the Court to know which officers were in charge of the identification procedures and whether they received appropriate training?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think the appropriate training is more important than the identity of the officers, but it would help, of course, to know who they were, what their experience was, how many there were, how they, sort of -- how it was ensured that they applied the same procedures consistently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Would it be helpful for the Court to know whether witnesses have described more suspects to the investigators and, if so, whether they were told which suspect they were asked to identify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
